quote: By far the best definition I’ve ever heard of the supernatural is Richard Carrier’s: A “supernatural” explanation appeals to ontologically basic mental things, mental entities that cannot be reduced to nonmental entities.
content: The definition is the standard one in philosophy of religion and philosophy of mind, and Carrier’s 2007 blog post is a late restatement of it. Draper’s widely cited formulation defines the natural as the physical and whatever is causally reducible to it and the supernatural as what is not (Draper, “God, Science, and Naturalism,” in The Oxford Handbook of Philosophy of Religion, 2005); Armstrong’s naturalism (1978) and Papineau’s (Philosophical Naturalism, 1993) locate the dividing line at the fundamentality of the mental; and the idea that the supernatural is the irreducibly mental is what Hume, Feuerbach and Freud were all attacking under the name of projection. The essay is correct to adopt it. The attribution matters only because the sequence repeatedly presents received distinctions as discoveries made on blogs, and a reader who wanted to follow the definition into the literature would not find it under Carrier’s name.

quote: Suppose that a 747 had a fundamental physical existence apart from the quarks making up the 747.
content: The question was answered in 1925. Broad’s The Mind and Its Place in Nature distinguished emergent from mechanistic laws by exactly the test the essay asks for: in a world with emergent (“configurational”) laws, the behaviour of a whole is not deducible from the behaviour of its parts in other configurations, and the observable signature is a failure of the microphysical laws to be closed, that is, a case where the parts do something in the configuration that the laws governing the parts alone do not predict. That is a prediction; it is the prediction that downward causation makes, and it is what every interactionist and strong-emergentist theory since has been tested against (Penrose’s Orch-OR is one such test, as the essay itself notes elsewhere). The essay says non-reductionism makes no predictions and is therefore incoherent; the tradition it is dismissing specified the predictions and has been losing on them, which is a different and better reason to reject it. There is also a tension internal to the essay: it argues that supernatural claims are not excluded a priori but refuted a posteriori (the Red Sea, the retina), and also that non-reductionism is “a confusion” with no envisionable content. A claim with no content cannot be refuted by archaeology; the essay wants the Bible’s Jehovah to be “coherent, falsifiable and wrong” and the irreducible Jehovah to be inconceivable, and switches between the two as the paragraph requires.

quote: likewise with the retina being designed backwards with the light-sensitive parts at the bottom; and so on through a thousand other items of evidence for splintered, immoral, incompetent design.
content: The inverted retina is the weakest of the thousand and Book III’s annotations on An Alien God gave the reasons: the Müller glial cells act as living optical fibres that guide light through the neural layers to the photoreceptors with little loss (Franze et al. (2007)), and the inverted arrangement places the photoreceptors against the pigment epithelium, which supplies their extraordinary metabolic demand and recycles the visual pigment; the cephalopod “right-way-round” retina that is offered as the better design has no fovea and lower acuity. The general point about poor design survives (the recurrent laryngeal nerve, the vas deferens, the human birth canal) and the Red Sea archaeology is sound (Finkelstein and Silberman, The Bible Unearthed, 2001). The retina is the example popular writers reach for because it sounds like a wiring error, and the ophthalmology says it is a trade-off; an essay about excluding hypotheses on the evidence should use the evidence that holds.

quote: Corollary: Any supposed designer of Artificial General Intelligence who talks about religious beliefs in respectful tones is clearly not an expert on reducing mental things to nonmental things; and indeed knows so very little of the uttermost basics, as for it to be scarcely plausible that they could be expert at the art; unless their idiot savancy is complete.
content: This is an argument from tone, of the kind Book II’s annotations found the book warning against, and it is empirically false as a test of competence. The people who actually built the systems that reduce mental-seeming behaviour to matrix multiplication held every view about religion, and some of the field’s founders were devout: Knuth is a Lutheran who wrote a book of lectures on faith and computation; Rosalind Picard, who founded affective computing, is an evangelical; the leadership of the laboratories that produced the current generation of language models includes practising members of several religions. “Respectful tones” toward a belief one does not share is also what the book elsewhere calls leaving a line of retreat, and it is compatible with thinking the belief false. The corollary would, applied in 2008, have excluded from expertise a good part of the people who went on to demonstrate the reduction the essay says they could not understand, and it says more about the author’s community than about the art.
